title: 长信秋词·其三
titlePy: Cháng Xìn Qiū Cí · Qí Sān
titleEn: Autumn Song of the Changxin Palace (No. 3)
author: 王昌龄
intro: A palace lady, forgotten by the emperor, sweeps the hall at dawn and envies the crows: they at least fly past the palace where he lives and carry its sunlight on their wings.
analysis: 这首诗写一位失宠的宫女。“长信”是汉代的长信宫，传说汉成帝的班婕妤失宠后到这里侍奉太后。诗的开头：天一亮宫殿开门，她就拿着扫帚去打扫，扫完无事可做，只好拿着团扇走来走去。团扇在古诗里常比喻被抛弃的女子——夏天离不开，秋天就被扔到一边。后两句是全诗最妙的地方：她白玉一样美的容颜，还比不上又黑又丑的寒鸦；因为寒鸦还能从昭阳殿（皇帝和宠妃住的地方）飞过来，身上带着那边的阳光。“日影”暗指皇帝的恩宠。用美人和乌鸦作对比，不直接说怨，怨却更深，这种写法叫“含蓄”。诗人借宫女的不幸，也写出有才能却不被重用的人的心情。
analysisEn: This poem is spoken for a palace lady who has lost the emperor’s favour. Changxin was a palace of the Han dynasty; the court lady Ban Jieyu is said to have gone there to serve the empress dowager after the emperor turned to a new favourite. At dawn the palace doors open and she takes her broom to sweep; with nothing else to do, she wanders up and down holding a round silk fan. In Chinese poetry such a fan stands for a woman cast aside — needed all summer, tossed away in autumn. The last two lines are the brilliant part: her jade-fair face is worth less than a cold black crow, because the crow can fly over from the Zhaoyang Palace, where the emperor and his favourite live, still carrying its sunlight on its wings. The “sunlight” is the emperor’s favour. Setting a beautiful woman against an ugly crow, the poem never complains outright, and the grief is all the deeper for it — Chinese critics call this hánxù, “holding back”. Through the palace lady, the poet also speaks for talented people who are passed over.
background: Wang Changling (c. 698–757) was famous for his seven-character quatrains, especially frontier poems and “palace laments” (宫怨) like this one. This is the third of five “Autumn Songs of the Changxin Palace”.
pronunciation: 奉帚 fèng zhǒu；团扇 tuán shàn；徘徊 pái huái；昭阳 zhāo yáng。
version: 采用《唐诗三百首》等通行文本（《唐诗三百首》题作《长信怨》）。“且将团扇”一作“暂将团扇”；“昭阳”，《全唐诗》作“朝阳”。

lines.py: fèng zhǒu píng míng jīn diàn kāi
lines.lit: Holding a broom at dawn, when the golden hall opens,
lines.en: At dawn the golden hall opens; I take up my broom,

lines.py: qiě jiāng tuán shàn gòng pái huái
lines.lit: for now I take my round fan and pace with it.
lines.en: then drift up and down with my round silk fan.

lines.py: yù yán bù jí hán yā sè
lines.lit: My jade face does not match the colour of the cold crows,
lines.en: My fair face counts for less than a black crow’s wing —

lines.py: yóu dài zhāo yáng rì yǐng lái
lines.lit: which still come carrying the sunlight of Zhaoyang Palace.
lines.en: the crows, at least, fly in with sunlight from his palace.

words.en: Changxin Palace, the empress dowager’s palace in Han times
to hold a broom — to sweep (a humble palace duty)

words.note: 古义“姑且”；今天多作“而且”。
古义“拿”，今天“将”多表示“把”或“将要”。
古诗里常比喻被抛弃的女子。
现代汉语仍用，也比喻犹豫不决。
现代汉语仍用，如“我不及他”。

words.en: Zhaoyang Palace, home of the emperor’s favourite
words.note: 后来泛指得宠妃子住的宫殿。
古代常以太阳比喻皇帝。

imagery.name: 扇
imagery.zh: 团扇秋天被丢在一边，正像失宠的宫女，被人遗忘。
imagery.en: A round fan put away in autumn — just like the lady, set aside and forgotten.

imagery.name: 鸦
imagery.zh: 又黑又丑的寒鸦还能飞过昭阳殿，美丽的人却不能，对比出宫女的凄凉。
imagery.en: Even an ugly black crow can fly past the emperor’s palace while she cannot — the contrast shows her desolation.
